newsitem.title: CANADA: Flax-fed chickens lay healthier eggs - researcher.
newsitem.headline: Flax-fed chickens lay healthier eggs - researcher.

text.p: Eggs produced by chickens fed on flaxseed could be healthier for people because of a particular type of polyunsaturated fat found in flax, a researcher told a meeting of the Flax Council of Canada here on Tuesday.

"Humans evolved on a diet much lower in fat and saturated fat compared to today's typical diet," said Artemis Simopoulos, president of the Center for Genetics, Nutrition and Health in Washington, D.C. "The diet of our ancestors contained small but roughly equal amounts of omega-6 and omega-3 polyunsaturated fats."
Flax is rich in omega-3 fat, she said, while dietary changes in the past 150 years have favoured omega-6 fats over omega-3.

"Today, we know that omega-3 fatty acids are essential for normal growth and development and may play an important role in the prevention and treatment of coronary artery disease, hypertension, diabetes, arthritis and cancer," she said.
Simopoulos cited a study showing that 25-gram yolks produced by flax-fed chicken contained 157.5 milligrams of omega-3 fat and 85 milligrams of omega-6.
That compared to supermarket eggs containing 30 milligrams of omega-3 amd 187.5 milligrams of omega-6.
The Flax Council pointed to the findings as a possible way to increase demand for flaxseed.

"With just a minor increase in market penetration by these omega-3 enriched eggs, demand for flax, from this industry alone, could reach more than 200,000 tonnes in the next decade," the council said.
World flax output in crop year 1995/96 (August/July) was 2.61 million tonnes, compared to 2.44 million tonnes in 1994/95. Canada is the world's leading flaxseed producer.
